body:
Finding Stability in a Life That Never Stands Still

Yosef · Yehudah and Tamar · Tiferes · Teshuvah

I. A Dvar Torah in the Middle of Moving

This week's Dvar Torah comes with a small apology built in. It may not be quite as polished or as fluid as usual, because we are, quite literally, in the middle of moving homes right now. But that is never an excuse not to share words of Torah. We always have to hold Torah close to us, close to our hearts and our minds, even in the words we speak in passing. If anything, it is precisely during life's busiest and most chaotic moments that we need Torah the most. Torah does not only belong in the Beis Midrash. It belongs in our homes, our conversations, our decisions, and our daily lives, especially when those homes are mid-move and those decisions are coming fast.

And in a strange way, that itself is the perfect introduction to Parshas Vayeishev.

II. Vayeishev: Settling, Then Everything Unravels

The parsha opens with the words:

וַיֵּשֶׁב יַעֲקֹב בְּאֶרֶץ מְגוּרֵי אָבִיו

"And Yaakov settled in the land where his fathers had lived."

— Bereishis 37:1

The very word vayeishev suggests stability, permanence, finally reaching a place of rest. Yet almost immediately, that sense of calm is shattered. Yosef is hated by his brothers, dreams create division, a sale into slavery takes place, Yehudah leaves his family, and one difficult episode follows another. How can a parsha that begins with settling become a parsha defined almost entirely by upheaval?

Perhaps the answer is that true stability is never determined by our surroundings. It is determined by where we place our trust.

III. Yosef's Reports, and the Question of Eiver Min HaChai

The central story is, of course, Yosef. We know his brothers were tzaddikim, which makes the entire episode harder to understand on its surface. How could tzaddikim commit such an act against their own brother? Chazal discuss at great length the complex halachic and moral questions surrounding the reports Yosef brought to Yaakov about his brothers, including the specific issue of eiver min hachai, whether the brothers had eaten from a live animal in a way that would have constituted a real violation. Yosef brought these reports to his father, in a manner that looked almost like tattling, genuinely believing he was doing what was right.

Yosef likely was acting from a sincere place. But he lacked the maturity and sensitivity with which truth sometimes needs to be presented. His close relationship with Yaakov had given him tremendous strengths, real closeness, real communication, but he had not yet developed the balance of Tiferes, the ability to combine truth with humility and compassion. That imbalance, more than any single report, is what created the friction that eventually led to everything that followed.

IV. What Stayed With Him Across the Distance

Years later, separated from his father by years and by an ocean of suffering, Yosef faces Potiphar's wife. And he resists. This is worth sitting with carefully, because Yosef had not seen Yaakov in a very long time at that point. He was alone, isolated, without the daily presence of the relationships that had shaped him. And yet the values and the strength that came from his relationship with his father remained with him, even across that distance. Healthy family relationships, once truly internalized, continue to influence a person even when the people themselves are far away or entirely out of reach.

Contrast that with Yehudah in the very same parsha. Yehudah approached a woman by the roadside, not realizing who she truly was, at a point in his life when he had become separated from his family and had lost the closeness and support that once guided him. Both men experienced distance from family. Only one of them had built something internal strong enough to hold under that distance.

V. Yosef Before Pharaoh: Real Teshuvah

Later still, after imprisonment, suffering, and isolation, Yosef stands before Pharaoh as a very different person. When Pharaoh asks him to interpret the dreams, Yosef could have claimed the credit for himself. Instead, his first response is:

בִּלְעָדָי אֱלֹקִים יַעֲנֶה אֶת שְׁלוֹם פַּרְעֹה

"It is not within me. Hashem will answer Pharaoh's welfare."

— Bereishis 41:16

The young man who once spoke openly about his own dreams, in a way that drew resentment from his brothers, now speaks only to magnify Hashem. The Midrash even teaches that Yosef demonstrated knowledge of every language spoken in the world at that moment. Yet rather than using that ability to elevate himself above Pharaoh, he exercised restraint. His greatness was no longer measured by what he could prove about himself, but by how faithfully he represented Hashem.

That is real growth. The Rambam famously explains that complete teshuvah occurs when a person encounters the very same situation again and responds differently. Yosef faced power once more, but this time without arrogance. He faced recognition, but without seeking honor. He faced opportunity, but used it only to sanctify Hashem's Name.

VI. Yehudah and Tamar: Owning the Truth

The parsha then turns to the story of Yehudah and Tamar. At first glance it feels like an interruption in the Yosef narrative. But it teaches the same lesson from another angle entirely. Yehudah, separated from his family and his support system, stumbles. And when the truth is finally revealed to him, he does not hide behind excuses or try to protect his own name. Instead, he declares:

צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי

"She is more righteous than I."

— Bereishis 38:26

That brief statement changes everything. Yehudah accepts responsibility. He owns his actions fully, without deflection. He allows the truth to transform him rather than defending himself against it. From that moment emerges not only personal growth, but ultimately the royal line of David HaMelech and, eventually, Mashiach himself.

VII. Failure as the Path, Not the Obstacle

Both Yosef and Yehudah experience real failure. Both undergo painful refinement. Both become greater specifically because they were willing to grow through adversity rather than run from it or bury it. This may be one of the most important lessons of Vayeishev.

Life will not always feel settled. Sometimes we ask ourselves, why did this happen to me. Sometimes we feel caught in circumstances we never would have chosen. Sometimes we make mistakes that leave us questioning who we are. And yet Yosef later tells his brothers that everything occurred exactly as Hashem intended, that they were merely the shluchim through whom Hashem's plan unfolded. That does not remove personal responsibility. The brothers remained responsible for their choices. Yehudah remained responsible for his choices. Yosef remained responsible for his own youthful mistakes in how he handled the truth. But alongside that responsibility stands another truth: Hashem is guiding history toward His purpose, even through our missteps.

Our task is not to understand every step immediately. Our task is to respond correctly to the step we are standing on today. We are not meant to surrender to our desires, and we are not meant to excuse our mistakes. But neither are we meant to remain trapped by them. Even our lowest moments can become opportunities for growth if they lead us closer to Hashem rather than further away.

VIII. Stability That Does Not Depend on Circumstances

As we enter Shabbos, perhaps that is the message worth carrying with us. The world around us is filled with movement, uncertainty, and unexpected turns. Families move homes. Careers change. Relationships are tested. Plans rarely unfold exactly as we expect. But a Jew's stability has never depended on having a perfectly stable life. Our stability comes from knowing Who walks beside us through every stage of the journey, even the stages that look nothing like vayeishev on the surface.

May we merit to strengthen our relationship with Hashem, to learn from both Yosef and Yehudah, to accept responsibility with humility, to recognize Hashem's hand even in life's unexpected turns, and to transform every challenge into another step toward greater kedushah.

חזק ואחזק

Shabbat Shalom

Reflection Questions

• Where in my life have I confused stability of circumstances with stability of trust? What would it mean to find calm even while things around me are still in motion?

• Like Yosef with his reports to Yaakov, is there a place where I am telling the truth but without the Tiferes, the balance of compassion and humility, that the moment actually calls for?

• What relationship or value, internalized long ago, has stayed with me and helped me resist something difficult, even when the person who gave it to me was far away or no longer present?

• Have I faced the same test twice and responded differently the second time, the way the Rambam describes as complete teshuvah? What did that actually look like?

• Like Yehudah, is there a truth in my own life I have been avoiding owning fully, where the honest words tzadkah mimeni still need to be said?

• Looking at a recent disruption or move in my own life, where do I see Hashem's hand guiding something I could not see clearly in the moment?
